newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Lebed, on NATO trip, takes West in stride.
newsitem.headline: Lebed, on NATO trip, takes West in stride.

text.p: Russian security chief Alexander Lebed, his face stoney and inscrutible and his voice as always a low growl, appeared to take the West in his stride when he flew in on Sunday to visit NATO's Brussels headquarters.

"I have no special feelings," he said, when asked about his first journey beyond the frontiers of the old Soviet Union except for his service in Afghanistan. "I feel comfortable wherever I am, including the West."

Lebed, a man in transition from four-star general to politician, had marked his arrival from the door of his airliner moments earlier with a raised arm caught somewhere between a stiff military salute and the beguiling politician's wave.

Wife on arm, swaddled securely in a heavy black trenchcoat despite warm Brussels sunshine, he walked down the steps with a dignity born of military ceremony to set foot for the first time on what for most of his army career had been enemy soil.

The official greetings over, with a courteous nod and booming "good afternoon" he walked up to waiting journalists and said he wanted to dispel misconceptions that were circulating about President Boris Yeltsin's security adviser.

"Some commentators of ill-will have been saying that Lebed is threatening NATO with nuclear weapons and saying Russia is ready to occupy some...countries if there is the slightest move of NATO to the east," he said.
These stories were, he said, like "the worst fairy tales of the Cold War."

Lebed's hair is dark and swept back, his nose a broad boxer's nose. He won fights as an amateur champion in his youth. His eyes are scarcely visible, set deep in their sockets behind heavy lids. His voice never wavers from the unstoppable rumble and, stopping short of a smile, he is courteous to a tee.

But commentators deserve some understanding for any confusion about the man who hopes to succeed Yeltsin as president. His comments have often been contradictory and, by the standards of conventional diplomacy, colourful.

"We have missiles which are rusty but still effective as a deterrent," Itar-Tass news agency quoted him as saying only last week. The image of rusting Russian rockets would be enough in itself to strike horror into the hearts of NATO experts.

Lebed was referring to NATO plans to embrace countries such as Poland, which once served Russian security interests in the now defunct Warsaw Pact. He has already denounced such expansion as a threat to Russian security.
He said he was visiting Brussels in search of civilised dialogue and with proposals to bury this dispute with NATO.

Many Western officials were watching Lebed's two-day visit with the same interest they devoted to Yeltsin on the foreign trips he made in the years before he eclipsed Mikhail Gorbachev as Kremlin chief in late 1991.

It is a first tentative encounter with a new political force. The 46-year-old Afghan veteran is, as Yeltsin was then, an unknown quantity. The West saw Gorbachev as the guarantor of democracy then and Yeltsin as a maverick who might threaten it.
Yeltsin, a skilled politician, later won the trust of the West. Lebed has no political career to draw on, but he is also no naive newcomer from the barracks.

He showed a keen talent for diplomacy as well as military strategy in using his 14th Army to defuse a conflict between Slavs and ethnic Romanians in Moldova. He also moved quickly to forge a peace in the rebel Chechnya region.
A popular, some say populist, leader, he performed strongly in the election which Yeltsin won earlier this year, prompting the Kremlin leader to bring him into his team.
But his support for Yeltsin in the second round won him the opprobrium of a communist-dominated parliament. He also has influential enemies in the government.
But confrontation is unlikely to discourage Lebed. "I was a born winner," he said in one interview.
As Yeltsin's heart bypass surgery approaches, Western officials must reckon with at least the possibility that this "born winner" might soon visit the West in a higher capacity.
